drivingQuestion: From where is it derived that blood that spurted and blood on the knife must be covered, and when does that obligation apply?
outcomeNote: A baraita is adduced in support of the mishna's clause; nothing is contested here.

segments.he: דָּם הַנִּיתָּז וְשֶׁעַל הַסַּכִּין, תָּנוּ רַבָּנַן: ״וְכִסָּהוּ״ – מְלַמֵּד שֶׁדַּם הַנִּיתָּז וְשֶׁעַל הַסַּכִּין חַיָּיב לְכַסּוֹת. אָמַר רַבִּי יְהוּדָה: אֵימָתַי? בִּזְמַן שֶׁאֵין שָׁם דָּם אֶלָּא הוּא, אֲבָל יֵשׁ שָׁם דָּם שֶׁלֹּא הוּא – פָּטוּר מִלְּכַסּוֹת.
segments.en: § The mishna teaches that one is obligated to cover «blood that spurts» outside the pit over which the animal was slaughtered, or onto the wall, «and» blood «that» remained «on the» slaughtering «knife.» With regard to this halakha, «the Sages taught» in a baraita: The verse states: «“And he shall cover it”» (Leviticus 17:13), which «teaches that» one is «obligated to cover blood that spurted and» blood «that» remained «on the» slaughtering «knife. Rabbi Yehuda said: When» is this the halakha? «When there is no blood except that» blood. «But» if «there is» other «blood that is not that» blood, one is «exempt from covering» it.
